opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a real shift for me. Before real-time voice, most of our evaluation thinking was built around text: you give the model a prompt, it gives you an answer, and you grade that answer. Even the harder evals, like multi-step reasoning or coding, still had that turn-based structure where you could pause and inspect each output.

With real-time voice, the interaction stops being a series of discrete answers and becomes something continuous. Suddenly things matter that we never had to measure before. How quickly does the model respond? Does it handle being interrupted gracefully? Does it pick up on tone? If someone sounds frustrated or hesitant, does the model notice and adjust? None of that shows up if you only look at a transcript.

It also made me think harder about the gap between what's easy to measure and what people actually experience. You can have a model that scores well on accuracy benchmarks but feels awkward to talk to, because the timing is off or it talks over you. So we had to think about evaluating the whole experience, not just the content.

And on the safety side, voice raised new questions. Can someone get the model to imitate a specific person's voice? Does it behave consistently when the same request comes in through audio instead of text? Your evaluations have to cover those modality-specific risks, because the failure modes really are different.

The bigger lesson for me was that as models become more capable and more embedded in how people actually interact with them, evaluations have to evolve too. We can't just keep reusing the same static benchmarks. We have to keep asking what really matters for the person on the other end, and then figure out how to measure that.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts real-time voice with the established text-based, turn-by-turn evaluation approach, including reasoning and coding tasks, and explains that continuous interaction requires evaluating new aspects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because I think before 4o, when we thought about evals, we were mostly thinking about text in, text out. You give the model a prompt, it gives you a completion, you grade the completion. And a lot of our eval infrastructure was built around that assumption, right? Static datasets, a scoring function, you run it and you get a number.

And then with real-time voice, a lot of those assumptions just broke. The first thing was latency. Suddenly it mattered not just whether the answer was correct, but whether it came back fast enough to feel like a conversation. If the model gives you a perfect answer but takes four seconds, that's a bad experience. So we had to start treating things like time-to-first-token as first-class metrics, not just things the infra team worried about.

The second thing was that the interaction became bidirectional and interruptible. In a text conversation, turns are very clean. In voice, people talk over each other, they change their minds mid-sentence, they say "um" and pause and the model has to decide whether they're done. So we had to start asking questions like, does the model handle interruptions gracefully? Does it know when to stop talking? Those are really hard to capture in a static benchmark, so we leaned much more heavily on human evaluation and on building simulated conversations where you actually play out multiple turns with realistic audio.

And then there's the stuff that's totally new to the modality. Tone, emotion, accents, background noise. Does the model understand someone who's speaking with a heavy accent, or in a noisy environment? Does it respond with the appropriate affect, like if someone sounds upset, does it pick up on that? We didn't have a vocabulary for evaluating that in the text world.

I think the bigger lesson for me was that evals have to follow the product. Every time the model gets a new capability or a new interface, you have to go back and ask, what does "good" actually mean here, and does my existing eval suite even measure it? And usually the answer is partially, at best. So it pushed us to be a lot more humble about our benchmarks and to invest more in things like red-teaming and real-world usage signals, because the thing you can measure in a lab is often not the thing that matters to the person actually talking to it.

r001.rationale: The response says real-time voice broke assumptions built around text-in/text-out evaluation, but it does not identify the prior paradigm as evaluating models through text and code on a computer.

astra-6.text:
It made me think about evaluation as something that has to happen at the level of a conversation. With text, you can look at a prompt and a response and ask, “Was that a good answer?” But in real-time voice, the experience also depends on when the model responds, whether it understands that you’re still speaking, and how it handles being interrupted. You can have a perfectly reasonable answer that feels wrong because it comes at the wrong moment.

So the question becomes: did the interaction work? Could you clarify something, change direction, or interrupt and still feel understood? That pushes you beyond evaluating individual answers toward evaluating how the model and the person navigate a conversation together.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text prompt-and-response evaluation with real-time conversational voice evaluation, but it does not identify code-based evaluation or evaluation on a computer as part of the established paradigm.

sol-6.1.text: It made me think about evaluation as an interaction, rather than just a question and an answer. With real-time voice, the model could give you the right information, but the experience could still feel wrong if it took too long to respond, interrupted you, or didn’t let you interrupt it. So you have to look at the whole conversation: Is it responding at the right moment? Is it following you when you change direction? Can it recover when it misunderstands? That broadens what it means for the model to do well.

r001.rationale: The response says voice evaluation should consider the whole interaction rather than just question and answer, but it does not identify a challenge to the established text-and-code-on-a-computer evaluation paradigm.
